title: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
summary: What runs under a vector query: SIMD distance kernels and horizontal sums, cache misses and prefetching in graph walks, immutable segments with tombstones and merges, WAL durability, mmap tiers and disk-based ANN.
outcomes: Compute FLOPs, bytes and cache lines per distance and explain why vector scans are memory-bound
Explain how SIMD distance kernels use lanes, FMA, multiple accumulators, horizontal sums and tails
Explain why graph traversal is dominated by cache misses and how layout and prefetching reduce them
Trace writes, deletes and merges through immutable segments, tombstone bitsets and compaction
Choose between in-memory, mmap and disk-based ANN designs, and explain how a WAL makes writes durable

lessons.title: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem

blocks.md: From the HNSW course you know that a query walks a proximity graph and computes the distance from the query to every neighbor it examines. A single query typically evaluates hundreds to thousands of such distances. This course is about what happens underneath that loop inside a vector database: the **distance kernel** (the tight function that computes one distance), how vectors and graph links sit in memory, how data is split into **segments** on disk, and how writes survive crashes.

Start with one distance between a query $q$ and a stored vector $x$, both 768-dimensional 32-bit floats (fp32), a common size for text embeddings.

- **Dot product** $\sum_i q_i x_i$: 768 multiplies and 767 adds, about $2d = 1{,}536$ floating-point operations (FLOPs).
- **Squared L2** $\sum_i (q_i - x_i)^2$: a subtract, a multiply and an add per dimension, about $3d = 2{,}304$ FLOPs.

The query is reused for every candidate, so it stays in the L1 cache. The stored vector is different each time and costs $4d = 3{,}072$ bytes to bring in.

blocks.caption: Arithmetic intensity: work done per byte fetched. It does not depend on d, so bigger embeddings do not help.

blocks.md: An intensity below 1 FLOP per byte is very low. A modern core with SIMD can do many FLOPs per cycle but can only pull a limited number of bytes per cycle from DRAM. Unless the vectors are already in cache, the core spends most of its time waiting for the 48 cache lines (64 bytes each) that make up one fp32 768-d vector.

blocks.title: One 768-d dot product: FLOPs versus bytes fetched

scenes.caption: fp32: 1,536 FLOPs against 3,072 bytes (48 cache lines). Intensity 0.5 FLOP per byte: the arithmetic is cheap, the data movement is not.
fp16 storage: the same 1,536 FLOPs, but only 1,536 bytes (24 lines). Intensity doubles to 1.0, so a memory-bound scan can do about twice as many distances.
int8 storage: 768 bytes (12 lines), intensity 2.0. This is why vector databases compress vectors; the product-quantization and RaBitQ courses go much further.

blocks.md: If memory bandwidth is the limit, throughput is simply bandwidth divided by bytes per vector. The plot below uses that model: it assumes every stored vector comes from DRAM and the query is cached.

blocks.title: Memory-bound ceiling: distances per second versus bandwidth

scenes.caption: At 20 GB/s, fp32 768-d vectors cap out at 20e9 / 3,072 = 6.5 million distances per second, no matter how fast the SIMD unit is. Simplified: real scans hit caches for part of the data.
Halving and quartering bytes per dimension doubles and quadruples the ceiling (13.0 and 26.0 million per second at 20 GB/s).
Doubling d to 1,536 halves every curve. Wider embeddings cost bandwidth linearly.

blocks.prompt: You port an exact (brute-force) scan over 768-d fp32 vectors from SSE (4 lanes) to AVX-512 (16 lanes). The dataset is 30 GB, far larger than the caches. What speedup do you expect?
blocks.reveal: Much less than 4x. The kernel now needs a quarter of the instructions, but each distance still needs 3,072 bytes from DRAM, and at 0.5 FLOP per byte the loop was already waiting on memory. Wider SIMD pays off fully only when data is in cache (small segments, hot graph regions) or when vectors are compressed so that more distances fit in each byte fetched.

blocks.md: At hundreds of dimensions, a distance does about 0.5 to 0.75 FLOPs per byte of vector it reads. SIMD makes the arithmetic cheap; after that, the bytes you move (and the cache misses you take) decide the speed.

A common mistake is to benchmark a distance kernel on a few thousand vectors that fit in L2 cache and extrapolate to a 100 GB index. The small benchmark measures compute; the real index measures memory.

blocks.question: Index A stores 1,536-d fp32 vectors. Index B stores 768-d int8 vectors. On a memory-bound scan, roughly how many more distances per second can B compute?
options: About the same, since both do one distance per vector
2x, because B has half the dimensions
8x, because B reads 768 bytes per vector instead of 6,144
4x, because int8 is a quarter of fp32
blocks.explain: Bytes per vector set the ceiling. A reads 1,536 x 4 = 6,144 bytes, B reads 768 x 1 = 768 bytes, a ratio of 8. Half the dimensions and a quarter of the bytes per dimension multiply.

blocks.question: Squared L2 has intensity 0.75 FLOP per byte and dot product 0.5. On a memory-bound scan, which runs faster per distance?
options: Dot product, because it does fewer FLOPs
About the same, because both read the same 4d bytes
L2, because higher intensity is always faster
Neither can be computed with SIMD
blocks.explain: When the limit is bytes, the extra subtract in L2 hides under the memory stall. Both read one 3,072-byte vector per distance, so their throughput is about equal.

lessons.title: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum

blocks.md:
The scalar loop `for (i...) s += a[i] * b[i]` handles one dimension per instruction. You already know SIMD registers hold several **lanes**: a 128-bit SSE or Arm Neon register holds 4 fp32 values, AVX2 (256-bit) holds 8 and AVX-512 holds 16.

Distance kernels also lean on **FMA** (fused multiply-add): one instruction computes $c + a \times b$ in every lane with a single rounding. A dot product is then just a stream of FMAs into an **accumulator** register, followed by one **horizontal sum** that adds the lanes together.

blocks.title: A 16-d dot product with 8 AVX2 lanes

scenes.caption: The accumulator starts at zero in all 8 lanes. Each lane will own every 8th dimension: lane 0 gets dimensions 0 and 8, lane 7 gets 7 and 15.
FMA 1 loads dimensions 0 to 7 of a and b and adds the products lane by lane: acc = (2, 2, 0, 1, 0, 2, 2, 2). One instruction, eight multiply-adds.
FMA 2 does dimensions 8 to 15 into the same register: acc = (4, 2, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 5). The loop is done; the answer is spread across 8 lanes.
Horizontal sum, step 1: add the upper 4 lanes to the lower 4 (4+3, 2+4, 2+2, 1+5) = (7, 6, 4, 6).
Step 2: add lanes 2 and 3 onto lanes 0 and 1: (11, 12).
Step 3: 11 + 12 = 23, which matches the scalar dot product. The reduction takes log2(8) = 3 add steps and runs once per distance, not once per dimension.

blocks.caption: A minimal AVX2 + FMA dot product. The final shuffles are the horizontal sum from the figure.

scenes.caption: Dot product: 768 / lanes FMA instructions. 192 for 4 lanes, 96 for 8, 48 for 16, plus a few for the horizontal sum.
Squared L2 needs a subtract and an FMA per group of lanes ($t = x - y$, then acc += $t \times t$), so twice the instructions: 1,536, 384, 192, 96.

blocks.md:
Real libraries differ in how they get there:

- **hnswlib** hand-writes intrinsics. Its AVX-512 inner product does four 16-lane FMAs per loop iteration (64 floats), all into a single accumulator register, so a 768-d vector takes exactly 12 iterations, then calls `_mm512_reduce_add_ps` for the horizontal sum. At index creation it picks AVX-512, AVX or SSE after checking the CPU.
- **FAISS** writes plain loops and lets the compiler vectorize them. The loops are wrapped in `FAISS_PRAGMA_IMPRECISE_FUNCTION_BEGIN`, which on GCC enables `associative-math` and on Clang turns precise floating point off, so the compiler may reorder the sum into lanes. Each kernel is compiled once per SIMD level (AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon, SVE and others), and a dynamic-dispatch build picks the highest level the CPU supports at run time.
- **Lucene** uses the Java Vector API with four independent FMA accumulators, then adds them and reduces the lanes.

Why four accumulators? Each FMA into the same register must wait for the previous one to finish (a dependency chain several cycles long). With four registers, four independent chains are in flight at once, which hides that latency. This matters most when vectors are in cache; when they come from DRAM the loads dominate anyway.

blocks.title: hnswlib with d = 770: SIMD body plus a scalar tail

scenes.caption: hnswlib chooses this residual version when d is not a multiple of 16 or of 4 and d is above 16. For d = 770 the body handles 768 elements.
The SIMD body processes 48 blocks of 16 floats.
Two elements are left over. They are handled by the plain scalar loop.
hnswlib returns 1 minus the dot product, so larger similarity means smaller distance. For d = 768 the residual step is skipped: 768 is a multiple of 16, so the pure SIMD16 kernel is used.

blocks.md: A scalar tail is not the only option. [NumKong](https://github.com/ashvardanian/NumKong) (the library formerly called SimSIMD) uses AVX-512 **masked loads**: for the last partial block it builds a lane mask with `_bzhi_u32` and loads with `_mm256_maskz_loadu_ps`, so missing lanes read as zero and no scalar loop is needed. Its AVX-512 f32 dot product also widens to fp64 before accumulating, trading speed for accuracy.

blocks.prompt: Take two random unit vectors in 768-d fp32. Compute their dot product (a) sequentially in fp32, (b) with 8 lane accumulators, (c) with 16 lane accumulators. Will the three answers be identical?
blocks.reveal: No. With a fixed random seed the fp64 reference was 0.041216347; sequential fp32 gave 0.041216370, 8 lanes 0.041216351 and 16 lanes 0.041216347. Floating-point addition is not associative, so every summation order rounds differently. The errors here are around $10^{-8}$, harmless for ranking in almost all cases, but two near-tied candidates can swap order between a scalar and a SIMD build. Tests should compare distances with a tolerance.

blocks.md: SIMD kernels are not bit-identical to the scalar loop. FAISS explicitly allows reassociation in its distance loops; that is a deliberate choice, not a bug. Do not assert exact equality of distances across CPUs or builds.
If your embeddings are normalized at insert time, cosine similarity equals the dot product, so the database can run the cheaper dot kernel and skip computing norms per distance.

blocks.question: A colleague's AVX-512 kernel uses one accumulator and runs 768-d distances on vectors that fit in L1. Splitting it into four accumulators makes it faster. Why?
options: Four accumulators halve the number of loads
Independent accumulators let several FMAs run in parallel instead of waiting on one dependency chain
AVX-512 cannot use a single register for more than 12 FMAs
Four accumulators avoid the horizontal sum
blocks.explain: Each FMA into the same register must wait for the previous result. Four independent chains keep the FMA units busy. Loads and the final reduction are unchanged (the reduction even gets slightly longer).

blocks.question: hnswlib builds an inner-product index with d = 100. Which kernel does it pick on an AVX machine?
options: The SIMD16 kernel with a 4-element scalar tail
The pure scalar loop
The SIMD4 kernel, since 100 is a multiple of 4
The AVX-512 kernel with a masked tail
blocks.explain: The dispatch checks d % 16 first, then d % 4. 100 is not a multiple of 16 but is a multiple of 4, so the SIMD4 kernel covers all 100 elements with no tail. The residual kernels are used only when neither divides d.

lessons.title: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching

blocks.md: A brute-force scan reads vectors in order, so the CPU's hardware prefetchers can stream them. A graph search is different: the neighbors of a node are arbitrary ids, so each new neighbor is at an unpredictable address in a large array. When the index is much bigger than the caches, almost every neighbor visit starts with a **cache miss**: the core stalls until the first line arrives from DRAM.

Because of that, the layout of a node in memory matters. **hnswlib** stores layer 0 (the bottom layer, which holds every vector) as one flat array of fixed-size blocks, one block per element, so element $i$ starts at $i$ times the block size. No pointers to chase: an id is enough to compute an address.

blocks.title: One hnswlib layer-0 block for M = 16, d = 768 fp32

scenes.caption: A 4-byte header: the neighbor count in its first 2 bytes, and a delete flag in byte 2 (used by markDelete).
Up to maxM0 = 2M = 32 neighbor ids at 4 bytes each: 128 bytes. Header plus links is size_links_level0_ = 132 bytes.
The raw vector starts at offsetData_ = 132: 768 x 4 = 3,072 bytes, which is 48 cache lines if aligned.
An 8-byte external label ends the block: 3,212 bytes in total. Since neither 132 nor 3,212 is a multiple of 64, the vector straddles 49 cache lines in 15 of every 16 blocks.

blocks.md: Two kinds of random access happen per neighbor: the **visited** check (hnswlib keeps an array of 16-bit tags, one per element, reused across queries by bumping the tag) and the neighbor's **vector**. hnswlib hides some of that latency with `_mm_prefetch`, a hint that asks the CPU to start loading a cache line now, before the code needs it. Its search loop prefetches the next neighbor's visited entry and vector while computing the current one. Prefetching is on by default and can be turned off by defining `HNSWLIB_USE_PREFETCH` as 0.

blocks.caption: The layer-0 search loop, simplified. Deleted nodes are still traversed but never enter the result set.

blocks.title: Visiting 4 neighbors with and without a one-ahead prefetch

scenes.caption: Toy model: a miss costs 100 ns, a distance 50 ns. Without prefetch each neighbor is load then compute, strictly in turn: 4 x 150 = 600 ns.
With hnswlib-style prefetch, neighbor j+1 is requested when work on neighbor j starts. Loads now overlap distances, and 4 neighbors finish at 350 ns.

Look-ahead of one is limited when a miss (100 ns) is longer than a distance (50 ns): in this model the CPU still idles 50 ns between pairs. Simplified: real CPUs keep many misses in flight and also prefetch sequential lines on their own.

blocks.md: Note what one `_mm_prefetch` covers: a single 64-byte line, the first of the roughly 48 lines in a 768-d fp32 vector. The rest of the vector is a sequential stream, which the hardware prefetchers are built to follow once the first lines are touched. This is another reason compressed vectors help graph search: fewer lines per hop means less exposed latency.

Other engines split the data differently. Lucene's HNSW format keeps the graph in a `.vex` file (per node, a count and delta-encoded neighbor ordinals) and the raw vectors in a separate flat `.vec` file. Its flat format aligns each field's vector data to 4,096 bytes, so a 1,024-d fp32 vector (exactly 4,096 bytes) never straddles a page, and notes that vectors whose size is not a multiple of 64 bytes end up unaligned for most entries, which can be slower on Arm Neoverse machines.

In graph search the expensive part per hop is often the first touch of a random vector, not the arithmetic. Contiguous fixed-size blocks, aligned vectors, prefetching and smaller (compressed) vectors all attack that same miss.

Deleting from hnswlib with `markDelete` only sets a flag. The node keeps its edges and is still used for routing; it is just filtered out of results. Lots of deletions therefore still cost traversal time until the index is rebuilt.

blocks.question: hnswlib prefetches `vector_of(data[j + 1])`. For a 768-d fp32 vector, what does that one instruction bring toward the cache?
options: All 3,212 bytes of the next neighbor's block
One 64-byte cache line at the start of the next neighbor's vector
The whole neighbor list of the next neighbor
Nothing on ARM builds without SSE, and everything on x86
blocks.explain: A prefetch hint covers the cache line containing the address. Here that is the first line of the vector. The remaining lines rely on the hardware stream prefetcher once the distance loop starts reading.

blocks.question: In the toy timeline, miss latency is 100 ns and a distance is 50 ns. Which change helps most?
options: Prefetching two or more neighbors ahead instead of one
Using AVX-512 to halve the 50 ns distance
Removing the visited-array check
Making the neighbor list longer
blocks.explain: The CPU waits because each load is issued only one distance (50 ns) before it is needed, but takes 100 ns. Issuing loads earlier overlaps more of the latency. Halving the compute time would make the stall share even larger.

lessons.title: Segments: immutable indexes, a write buffer, tombstones and merges

blocks.md: Updating an HNSW graph in place is awkward. An insert must search the graph and rewire neighbor lists that concurrent readers are walking. A delete leaves a hole that other nodes route through. And a big graph is expensive to rewrite on disk for every small change.

Most vector databases borrow the answer from search engines and LSM trees: **segments**.

1. New writes go to a small mutable **write buffer**.
2. When it is big enough it is frozen into an **immutable segment** with its own vector index, written once.
3. A query searches every segment and merges the per-segment top-k lists.
4. Deletes only set a mark (a **tombstone**). Background **merges** (also called compaction) rewrite several segments into one, dropping deleted rows.

blocks.title: Write buffer, immutable segments, fan-out query and merge

scenes.caption: A write is logged durably, then applied to the mutable buffer. Readers never see a half-built graph in an immutable segment.
Flush: the buffer is frozen into segment 3 and its index is built once. A fresh empty buffer takes new writes.
A query runs on every segment (and the buffer) in parallel; each returns its own top-k and a final step keeps the global best k.
Many small segments mean many small searches per query, so a background merge rewrites segments 1 and 2 into one larger segment and drops their deleted rows.
After the merge, the old segments are released and queries fan out to fewer, larger segments.

blocks.md:
The same shape appears under different names:

- **Lucene** (and Elasticsearch and OpenSearch on top of it): each segment is a fully independent index; the index evolves by creating new segments and merging existing ones. Documents are buffered in RAM (16 MB by default) and flushed as new segments. Segments too small to benefit (an expected search effort under 100 visited nodes) get no HNSW graph at all.
- **Qdrant**: a collection is a set of segments, each with its own vector and payload storage and indexes. Segments are **appendable** or **non-appendable** (read and delete only), and at least one appendable segment must exist.
- **Milvus**: **growing** segments hold data not yet persisted to object storage; a flush turns them into **sealed** segments, which are immutable and indexed one by one.
- **Lance** (LanceDB's format): rows live in **fragments**; each version of the table is an immutable manifest listing them.

blocks.prompt: A collection has 4 segments and you ask for the top 10. A teammate suggests asking each segment for its top 3 to save work (12 candidates total). What goes wrong?
blocks.reveal: If 6 of the true global top 10 live in one segment, that segment only returns 3 of them, and the answer silently loses 3 good results. Each segment must return its own top 10 (or more, since ANN within a segment is already approximate) before the global merge.

blocks.md:
**Deletes as tombstones.** Rewriting an immutable segment to remove one row is too expensive, so engines record which rows are dead:

- Lucene writes an optional `.liv` file per segment, a bitset of live documents stored as 64-bit words. For 1,000,000 documents that is 15,625 words, 125,000 bytes.
- Lance stores a **deletion file** per fragment: a flat list of deleted row offsets (Arrow IPC, good for sparse deletes) or a compressed roaring bitmap (good for dense deletes). Readers must filter those rows.
- Qdrant marks records as deleted instead of removing them immediately, to avoid slow disk operations during queries.

blocks.title: Toy merge: live bits, deletes and renumbering

scenes.caption: Two immutable segments, A with 5 vectors and B with 3. Positions are segment-local ordinals; the graph inside each segment uses them.
Deleting a1, a4 and b2 writes no vector data. Only the live bits flip to 0; searches skip these rows in results.
A merge copies only live rows and renumbers them densely: a0, a2, a3, b0, b1 become ordinals 0 to 4. A freshly merged segment has no gaps and no tombstones.

Lucene does not rebuild the graph from scratch: it reuses the graph with the most live vectors and at most 40% deletions as the base. A has 2 of 5 deleted, exactly 40%, so it qualifies; its deleted nodes are skipped and nodes that lost neighbors are repaired.
B also has a deletion, so its graph is not merged in; b0 and b1 are inserted into the base graph the normal way. A deletion-free segment would instead be joined with cheaper, seeded searches.

blocks.md:
**When to merge or vacuum** is a policy question. Qdrant documents three optimizers:

- The **vacuum optimizer** rewrites a segment once at least `deleted_threshold` (0.2 in the example config) of its records are deleted and it has at least `vacuum_min_vector_number` (1,000) vectors. A segment of 5,000 vectors with 1,200 deleted is at 24%, so it qualifies.
- The **merge optimizer** keeps the segment count near `default_segment_number` (by default chosen from the CPU count) and may merge the three smallest segments; `max_segment_size_kb` caps segment size because large segments take longer to index.
- The **indexing optimizer** builds a vector index once a segment passes `indexing_threshold_kb` (default 10,000 KB of vectors; Qdrant counts 1 KB as one 256-d fp32 vector, so about 3,333 vectors at 768-d). Below it, a plain brute-force scan is used.

During optimization the segment stays readable behind a proxy; new changes go to a copy-on-write segment.

Immutable segments turn random in-place updates into sequential writes plus background rewrites. The price is read amplification: every query touches every segment, and dead rows cost time until a merge removes them.

Tombstoned vectors are not free. They still occupy memory, and in a graph they are still traversed for routing. Heavy delete or update workloads need merges (and their CPU cost for rebuilding graphs) or latency and memory creep up.

blocks.question: Qdrant's vacuum example config uses deleted_threshold 0.2 and vacuum_min_vector_number 1000. Which segment is vacuumed?
options: 800 vectors, 400 deleted
50,000 vectors, 5,000 deleted
2,000 vectors, 500 deleted
All three, since all have deletions
blocks.explain: 800 vectors is below the 1,000 minimum, even at 50% deleted. 50,000 with 5,000 deleted is only 10%. 2,000 with 500 deleted is 25%, above 20%, with enough vectors.

blocks.question: Why do segment-based engines usually skip building an HNSW graph for very small segments?
options: Small segments cannot be stored on disk
A brute-force scan over a few thousand vectors is about as fast as a graph search and avoids the build cost
HNSW requires at least one million vectors
Small segments are always deleted before they are searched
blocks.explain: Lucene skips the graph when the expected visited nodes are under 100, and Qdrant uses a plain index below its indexing threshold. For tiny segments the exact scan is cheap, exact, and costs nothing to build.

lessons.title: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN

blocks.md: The write buffer lives in memory, so a crash would lose it. The standard fix is a **write-ahead log** (WAL): an append-only file where every change is recorded, and flushed to stable storage, before it is acknowledged. After a crash the system replays the log to rebuild whatever was not yet in a persisted segment.

Qdrant documents exactly this two-stage path. A change is first written to the WAL, which orders all operations and gives each a sequential number; once in the WAL it will not be lost even on power loss. Then it is applied to segments. Each segment records the last applied version and the version of each point, and the updater **ignores a change whose number is lower than the point's current version**. That rule makes replay safe: re-applying an old log entry cannot overwrite newer data.

blocks.title: WAL, apply, crash and replay with point versions

scenes.caption: Upsert of point P is appended to the WAL as operation 41 before anything else happens.
Once the log append is durable the client can be acknowledged, even though no index has changed yet.
Ops 41 and 42 (another upsert of P) are applied; the segment persists P at version 42. Op 43 is logged but the process crashes before applying it.
On restart the WAL is replayed. Op 41 is older than P's version 42, so it is ignored; op 43 is newer and is applied. No data lost, nothing applied twice in the wrong order.

blocks.md: Milvus follows the same idea at cluster scale: a Streaming Node assigns each operation a timestamp from a timestamp oracle, writes it to the WAL, and can replay the WAL after a crash; it then cuts committed entries into **growing** segments and flushes them into **sealed**, immutable segments in object storage. Lucene by itself has no WAL: `IndexWriter.flush()` writes in-memory segments to the directory without fsync, and only `commit()` syncs the files so changes survive an OS crash or power loss. The [IndexWriter source](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/main/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/index/IndexWriter.java) also warns that some devices acknowledge fsync before data is truly stable.

**mmap versus in-memory.** Once a segment is immutable it is just files, and engines can memory-map them: the OS page cache holds the hot parts and a page fault reads the rest from disk.

- Qdrant always stores vectors in a memory-mapped file and offers a memory tier per vector: **cached** (the default, pre-loaded into the page cache at startup, needs enough RAM) or **cold** (not pre-loaded; first reads go to disk).
- Milvus can mmap vector data, vector indexes and scalar data per field; its docs warn that when data exceeds memory by too much, search performance can degrade seriously.
- Lucene's `FSDirectory.open` returns an `MMapDirectory` on 64-bit Linux, macOS, Solaris and Windows.

blocks.title: Toy model: average vector access time as RAM shrinks

scenes.caption: 10 million 768-d fp32 vectors are 30.72 GB. Assume 0.1 us from RAM, 100 us per SSD read and uniform access. With all data cached, each access is 0.1 us.
With 16 GB, 52% of accesses hit: the average jumps to 48 us, nearly 500x slower. A few misses dominate because one SSD read costs as much as 1,000 RAM reads.
Compressing to int8 (7.68 GB) puts everything back in RAM at 16 GB. Simplified: real access is skewed toward hot nodes, which helps, and graph hops each wait on a read, which hurts.

blocks.md: **Disk-based ANN.** mmap treats the SSD as slow RAM and hopes the working set fits. Disk-native indexes instead design for the SSD. The DiskANN paper keeps **compressed** (product-quantized) vectors of every point in RAM and stores the graph plus the **full-precision** vectors on the SSD, each node's neighbor list next to its vector. Search steers with the compressed distances, reads a **beam** of W nodes per round trip (reading several random sectors costs about as much as one), and uses the full-precision vectors it fetched along the way to re-rank. It reports indexing a billion points on one machine with 64 GB of RAM, serving over 5,000 queries per second at under 3 ms mean latency with 95%+ 1-recall@1 on SIFT1B.

blocks.title: DiskANN-style split between RAM and SSD (high level)

scenes.caption: Compressed codes for every point sit in RAM, so approximate distances never touch the SSD.
The search keeps a frontier and picks the W most promising unexplored nodes.
W node blocks are read in parallel in one round trip. A 768-d fp32 vector (3,072 bytes) plus 64 neighbor ids (256 bytes) is about 3.3 KB, so one node fits in a single 4 KB sector.
Full vectors that came along with the neighbor lists are used to re-rank, fixing the error of the compressed distances at no extra I/O.

blocks.md: The diskann-cagra course covers Vamana graph construction and the GPU side in depth. For this course, the takeaway is the design pattern: keep a small, compressed representation in RAM for navigation, put the bulky exact data where it is cheap, and lay it out so each random read fetches everything one step of the search needs.

Durability comes from the log, not the index: indexes are rebuilt or replayed from the WAL. Speed comes from what fits in RAM: keep the navigation data (graph upper layers, compressed vectors) in memory, and make every disk read count.

Turning on mmap does not shrink an index; it only lets the OS evict parts of it. If the hot working set does not fit, latency can fall off a cliff, because each miss is a disk read instead of a DRAM access.

blocks.question: A Qdrant point is at version 42 in a segment. During WAL replay the server sees op 40 (an upsert of that point). What happens?
options: It is applied, because replay must re-execute every logged operation
It is ignored, because its sequence number is lower than the point's current version
The segment is rebuilt from scratch
Replay stops with a corruption error
blocks.explain: The documented rule is to ignore a change whose sequential number is less than the point's current version. That makes replaying the whole log idempotent with respect to already-applied newer state.

blocks.question: Your 768-d fp32 index needs 31 GB and the machine has 16 GB for page cache. Which change most directly attacks the latency cliff?
options: Switch the vectors to the cached tier so they are pre-loaded at startup
Use a faster SIMD instruction set
Increase the number of segments
Compress the vectors (for example to int8 or PQ codes) so the navigation data fits in RAM, and re-rank with full vectors
blocks.explain: Pre-loading cannot fit 31 GB into 16 GB, and SIMD speed is irrelevant when waiting on the SSD. Shrinking what the search touches per hop, and reading exact vectors only for the final re-rank, is exactly the DiskANN-style pattern.

sources.label: Lance table format: fragments and deletion files
